article_blocks.text: Strain Type: 70% Indica / 30% Sativa
Genetics: Lemon Kush Bx3 × Humboldt Gelato
Breeder: Humboldt Seed Company
THC Content: 25–30%
CBD Content: Low
Terpene Profile: N/A
Primary Flavors: Lemon, lime, sour citrus, fuel, light cream
Flowering Time (Indoor): Approximately 50 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: September 20 – October 5
Indoor Yield: High
Outdoor Yield: High
Grow Difficulty: Easy to intermediate

Lemongrass does not whisper citrus. A mature flower can smell as though someone crushed lemon-drop candy over fresh lime peel and then spilled gasoline nearby. Humboldt Seed Company deliberately pushed the cultivar toward that collision of sharp fruit and fuel, creating marijuana whose aroma is brighter than its 70% indica classification would suggest. The buds form densely along large, vigorous plants, with relatively little excess leaf obscuring the flowers. By harvest, the lime-green surfaces are heavily resinous, while the sharp sour-citrus bouquet can become strong enough to dominate a grow room before the plant is even cut.

Its agricultural performance is just as important as the terpene profile . Humboldt developed the line for growers who needed large plants, substantial harvests, rapid flowering, and enough resilience to withstand real outdoor pressure. Indoor bloom takes only about 50 days, and outdoor maturity generally arrives between September 20 and October 5. Mold, mildew, and disease resistance are specifically emphasized by the breeder, making this hybrid particularly useful in gardens where late-season moisture can punish more delicate genetics. Despite the indica-dominant classification, the experience is notably energetic and euphoric, creating a striking contrast between the plant’s genetic ratio and the way its effects often unfold.
Genetics and Lineage

Humboldt Seed Company developed Lemongrass from Lemon Kush Bx3 × Humboldt Gelato. The current breeder catalog identifies the stabilized commercial line as F3, reflecting continued selection beyond the original parental combination. Lemon Kush Bx3 provides the dominant citrus character, including sour lemon, lime, and fuel-like pungency. Repeated backcrossing of the Lemon Kush side helped concentrate those traits before it entered the final cross, giving the finished cultivar the unmistakable acidic aroma that inspired its name.

Humboldt Gelato contributes a different set of qualities. Dense flowers, potency, resin production, and a smoother sweet or creamy background all help round out the sharper Lemon Kush influence. Gelato-derived genetics can sometimes produce compact plants with more demanding growth habits, but Lemongrass was selected in the opposite direction: large plants, strong hybrid vigor, substantial branching, and reliable production. The finished weed therefore carries Gelato richness without behaving like a small boutique dessert strain .

Continued selection also concentrated practical agricultural characteristics. Humboldt favored plants that remained healthy under mold and disease pressure while producing dense flowers with a low leaf-to-bud ratio. That combination matters for commercial cultivation because flowers can be processed efficiently by hand or machine without excessive leafy material. The lineage is therefore best understood not simply as lemon genetics crossed with Gelato, but as a breeding project aimed at bringing sharp citrus terpenes, high potency, vigorous field performance, and rapid maturation into one dependable plant.
Effects and Experience

The high often contradicts what consumers expect from a 70% indica hybrid. Instead of opening with immediate heaviness, the first phase can feel bright, euphoric, and mentally active. Mood may lift quickly, conversation can become more animated, and creative or recreational activities may feel easier to become absorbed in. Humboldt characterizes the effect as energizing and highly potent, making the cultivar better aligned with an active afternoon than its indica percentage alone would suggest.

Physical relaxation generally remains underneath the cerebral component rather than taking control from the beginning. Muscular tension may soften while the mind stays engaged, producing a comfortable balance between stimulation and calm. Moderate consumption can therefore feel surprisingly functional for experienced consumers. Larger servings change the equation considerably, however. At 25–30% THC, concentration can become scattered, reaction time declines, and the initial uplift may transition into heavier intoxication even without classic couch-lock.

That potency warrants caution. Strong examples can cause anxiety, dizziness, dry mouth, short-term memory disruption, or an uncomfortable sense of mental acceleration when consumed beyond personal tolerance. The energetic reputation should never be interpreted as evidence that the strain improves objective productivity or concentration. Cannabis impairment remains present even when the person feels alert, creative, or motivated.
Medical Benefits

An uplifting experience accompanied by relatively mild body relaxation may interest medical marijuana consumers who prefer avoiding immediate sedation. Cannabis with similar subjective characteristics is sometimes selected by people dealing with persistent discomfort, appetite changes, or symptoms that make heavily sedating weed impractical during the day. The brighter mental effect may also feel preferable to consumers who dislike the sluggishness produced by strongly narcotic indica cultivars.

Lemongrass itself has not been evaluated in controlled clinical trials as a treatment for depression, anxiety, chronic pain, fatigue, nausea, ADHD, or another medical condition. Research involving cannabis and cannabinoids more broadly supports potential usefulness for certain forms of chronic pain and nausea, but results depend on the cannabinoid formulation, dosage, delivery method, and patient population. Those findings cannot automatically be applied to a specific high-THC flower.

The 25–30% THC range can also create medical drawbacks. Sensitive consumers may experience increased anxiety, dizziness, cognitive impairment, or excessive stimulation. Cannabis may interact with certain prescription medications and can impair coordination even when it does not feel physically heavy. Medical use should therefore be based on current laboratory testing, careful dosing, and appropriate professional guidance rather than the strain’s uplifting reputation alone.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Fresh lemon dominates immediately, but the profile has more acidity than sweetness. The smell can resemble lemon drops, lime peel, and freshly squeezed citrus layered over pungent fuel. A sour edge gives the bouquet an almost mouthwatering sharpness, while earthy resin underneath prevents it from becoming a simple lemon-candy strain. When flowers are broken apart, the gasoline component becomes stronger and gives the aroma considerably more weight.

Flavor follows the same basic architecture with a little more softness. Lemon and lime appear early on the palate, followed by sour resin and fuel. Certain phenotypes may reveal a mild creamy quality inherited from Humboldt Gelato, although it usually remains behind the citrus instead of dominating the experience. The finish can become earthy and slightly pungent, creating a progression from bright fruit toward heavier cannabis resin.

Humboldt does not publish a permanent compound-by-compound terpene profile for every Lemongrass plant. Citrus-heavy expressions would reasonably be expected to contain substantial citrus-associated terpenes such as limonene, but exact rankings and percentages require batch-specific laboratory testing. Growing conditions and post-harvest treatment also influence aromatic chemistry. Excessive drying temperatures can quickly destroy the brightest lemon and lime notes, leaving the finished flower much more fuel-heavy than the living plant.
Growing Information

Lemongrass was bred to become large. Humboldt describes significant hybrid vigor, with plants capable of developing rapidly into productive specimens carrying abundant dense flowers. Indoors, that vigor deserves planning before flowering begins. Plants with unrestricted vegetative growth can occupy considerable canopy space, so topping, branch positioning, or other forms of early canopy management may be useful where cultivation is legal and vertical room is limited.

Flowering takes approximately 50 days according to the breeder’s current specifications, making the cultivar exceptionally fast for such a vigorous plant. Humboldt rates indoor and outdoor production as high, although no universal grams-per-square-meter or grams-per-plant number is attached to the current breeder specifications. Final harvest weight depends on root volume, light intensity, climate, vegetative time, plant density, and overall cultivation conditions.

Flower structure is one of the plant’s strongest commercial characteristics. Buds develop densely but carry comparatively little surrounding leaf, giving mature plants a favorable flower-to-leaf ratio. That structure simplifies hand trimming and also makes the cultivar suitable for mechanical processing. Strong branches support substantial flower development, while heavy resin coverage adds visual appeal to the final harvest.

Perhaps the most useful trait is environmental resilience. Humboldt specifically highlights resistance to disease, mildew, and mold, and the cultivar appears on the breeder’s list of mold-resistant photoperiod strains. That resistance expands its usefulness outdoors, particularly in regions where morning dew or early-autumn humidity can threaten dense cannabis flowers. It should not be interpreted as immunity; generous spacing, airflow, moisture management, and regular inspection remain important.

Outdoor plants generally mature between September 20 and October 5. That relatively early finish allows large plants to be harvested before many regions enter their wettest autumn period. Combined with natural disease resistance, the schedule gives growers two layers of protection against late-season losses. Once harvested, gradual drying is especially important for preserving the volatile lemon and lime aroma. A patient cure integrates the sour citrus with fuel and cream while maintaining the dense flower’s resinous character.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Lemongrass?
Humboldt Seed Company bred Lemongrass from Lemon Kush Bx3 × Humboldt Gelato. The current breeder catalog identifies the stabilized commercial line as F3.
Is Lemongrass indica or sativa?

The breeder classifies the cultivar as approximately 70% indica and 30% sativa. Despite that ratio, the effects are commonly energetic, euphoric, and mentally uplifting rather than immediately sedating.
How strong is Lemongrass?
Humboldt lists approximately 25–30% THC. Actual potency varies according to phenotype, cultivation conditions, harvest maturity, and laboratory methodology.
What does Lemongrass taste like?
The primary profile combines lemon drops, lime, sour citrus, and fuel. Some flowers also reveal light creamy or earthy characteristics inherited from the Humboldt Gelato side.
How long does Lemongrass take to flower?
Indoor flowering takes approximately 50 days. Outdoors, Humboldt lists a harvest window from roughly September 20 through October 5 in suitable Northern Hemisphere climates.
Final Thoughts on Lemongrass

Lemongrass stands out because nearly every major trait points toward practical performance without sacrificing a distinctive sensory identity. Lemon Kush Bx3 supplies the sharp citrus and sour fuel, while Humboldt Gelato adds dense flower formation, potency, resin, and a softer background. Continued F3 selection refined those qualities into a weed strain that grows with far more vigor than many boutique Gelato-derived hybrids.

The cultivation profile is unusually efficient. About 50 days of flowering, high production, large plants, a low leaf-to-flower ratio, and strong mold and disease resistance create a combination suited to both smaller gardens and larger-scale production. An early outdoor finish further reduces the amount of time dense flowers spend exposed to worsening autumn weather.

For consumers, the contrast between genetics and experience may be the most interesting characteristic. Although the plant is 70% indica, the high tends to begin bright, euphoric, and energetic. Sharp lemon, lime, sourness, and gasoline reinforce that lively personality, while enough physical relaxation remains underneath to keep the effect balanced. Lemongrass ultimately succeeds because the name describes only part of what makes it memorable: behind the intense citrus is a fast, vigorous, potent, and unusually resilient Humboldt cultivar.
